A delinquent is a person — almost always a young person — who repeatedly behaves in ways that break rules, laws, or the basic standards of acceptable conduct in society.

Think of it this way: most people, when they make a mistake or break a small rule, do it once and move on. A delinquent is someone who makes a pattern out of it. The word doesn't just describe a single bad act — it describes a person whose behavior has become a consistent problem for those around them and, often, for the law.

The classic phrase you'll encounter almost everywhere is "juvenile delinquent." "Juvenile" simply means young person, and this phrase is the bread-and-butter use of the word. When someone says juvenile delinquent, they mean a young person (typically a teenager or pre-teen) who regularly gets into trouble — with teachers, with neighbours, with the police, or with the law.
What Kind of Behaviour Makes Someone a Delinquent?

This is important: the word sits in a specific middle ground. A delinquent is not a hardened criminal. The acts are usually minor to moderate in severity — bad enough to be a real problem, but not the worst things imaginable. Common examples include:

  • Stealing small items (shoplifting)
  • Vandalizing property (graffiti, breaking things)
  • Skipping school repeatedly (truancy)
  • Getting into fights
  • Trespassing
  • Harassing others
  • Disobeying authority figures habitually

You would not typically call a person who commits a very serious crime like murder or armed robbery simply a "delinquent." That word would feel oddly mild. Delinquent implies a certain level of trouble — serious enough to be noticed and dealt with, but it still leaves open the possibility that the person could be corrected or rehabilitated.
The Judgment Packed Into the Word

The word "delinquent" is not neutral. It carries a clear negative judgment. When someone is called a delinquent, the speaker is communicating:

  • This person is irresponsible and refuses to follow the rules that everyone else follows.
  • This person is a problem — for the family, the school, the community, or society.
  • This person has failed to meet basic duties and obligations, particularly the duty to behave lawfully and decently.

It also carries a slight sense of disappointment — as if the person should know better but is choosing not to. This is partly why the word is so commonly applied to young people: there is an unspoken idea that they are capable of doing better, but are currently going in the wrong direction.

In law — especially in the legal systems of the United States, the United Kingdom, India, and many other countries — "delinquent" has a specific technical meaning. A juvenile delinquent is a minor (a person below the legal age of adulthood) who has committed an act that would be considered a crime if carried out by an adult.

The legal system treats these individuals differently from adult criminals. There are separate courts (often called Juvenile Courts or Family Courts), and the goal is typically correction and rehabilitation rather than punishment alone. The law recognizes that young people are still developing, and the label "delinquent" in this context is meant to trigger a different, more corrective kind of response from the system.

Occasionally, yes — but it's much rarer and feels slightly old-fashioned or literary when used this way. An adult might be called a "delinquent" in a somewhat informal or cutting tone to suggest they are behaving irresponsibly and refusing to meet their obligations, almost like a misbehaving child. It's used more as a dig than as a serious label. In practice, when adults break the law, the world tends to use words like criminal, offender, or convict instead.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Understanding where "delinquent" sits among related words will sharpen your grasp of it:

  • Criminal — A criminal is anyone who commits a crime, regardless of age. The word is broader and more serious in tone. All juvenile delinquents commit criminal acts, but calling a teenager a "criminal" sounds harsher and more final than calling them a "delinquent."
  • Offender — An offender is someone who has committed a specific offense. It is a more clinical and legal-sounding word, used across all age groups, and doesn't carry the same repeated-pattern implication.
  • Troublemaker — This is a milder, more informal word. A troublemaker might just be mischievous or annoying. A delinquent has gone further — their behaviour crosses into lawbreaking or serious rule-breaking.
  • Hooligan / Thug — These are informal words with more aggressive flavour, often implying physical menace. "Delinquent" is more neutral in register and is used in formal, legal, and everyday contexts alike.

Here are sentences that show how the word is used as a noun:

  1. The school had set up a special programme to help young delinquents get back on the right track.
  2. He was labelled a juvenile delinquent at fifteen after being caught vandalizing the local park for the third time.
  3. The judge ordered the delinquent to perform community service rather than serve time in a youth detention centre.
  4. Growing up in a tough neighbourhood, he fell in with a group of delinquents who regularly broke into shops.
  5. The social worker believed that with the right support, even the most hardened young delinquent could turn their life around.

The word is used across a wide range — in formal legal documents, in newspaper articles, in academic writing, and in everyday conversation. In formal contexts (law, social work, journalism), it is used straightforwardly and descriptively. In informal conversation, it can sometimes be used with a hint of sarcasm or humour — for example, a parent might jokingly call their messy, rule-bending teenager "a little delinquent," without meaning it in a fully serious legal sense.

When someone is labelled a delinquent, it is rarely just a factual description. It also signals a kind of social alarm — a warning that this person, if not helped or corrected, may go on to become a more serious criminal. The word sits at a crossroads between a current problem and a possible future one. This is why conversations around juvenile delinquency often involve not just punishment, but causes (poverty, broken homes, lack of education, peer pressure) and solutions (counselling, mentoring, community programmes).

In short, the word "delinquent" as a noun describes a person — primarily a young one — who has stepped outside the boundaries of lawful and socially acceptable behaviour in a persistent way, earning both society's concern and its disapproval, while still leaving the door open to the hope of change.
